title: Egypt's Mummified Cats Lived Hard Lives, Skulls Show
paragraphs: Cats held a sacred status in ancient Egypt, and huge numbers were mummified as offerings. It is natural to assume that such animals were treated well in life, but a new study of their skulls challenges that picture.

Wim Van Neer and Bea De Cupere, of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, examined 131 mummified cat skulls from Beni Hassan and reported their findings in the Journal of Archaeological Science. Fourteen skulls showed injuries, nineteen had small holes in the eye sockets that may reflect infection or nutritional stress, and about 86 percent of the animals were adults, compared with roughly 20 percent in earlier studies of cat mummies. "This is not what one would expect for animals destined to become votive mummies," De Cupere said. Some wounds appear to have been made by a sharp metal object, and the authors link the evidence to crowded living conditions that could have fuelled stress, aggression and the spread of disease.

Several caveats apply. Only skulls were available, which makes diagnosis harder than it would be with complete skeletons, and the intent behind the violence is unclear: a fatal blow could have preceded mummification, while healed wounds show that some animals survived. The study does not prove that the Egyptians were careless owners.

questions.q: What proportion of the cats were adults, and why is it notable?
questions.a: About 86 percent, compared with roughly 20 percent in earlier studies.

questions.q: What do the authors link the evidence to?
questions.a: Crowded living conditions that may have caused stress, aggression and disease.

questions.q: Why can the researchers not say who caused the wounds?
questions.a: Only skulls were available and the intent behind the violence is unclear.
